scenarios._comment: Hand-maintained metadata contract for the VelocityBench site. Changes only when the benchmark grid changes. Exclusion reasons are verbatim from docs/scenarios.md; framework/scenario orders are canonical (do not derive from dict order).

fraiseql-tv.note: precomputed tv_* tables, no result cache

fraiseql-v-nocache.note: on-the-fly JSONB JOIN views, no result cache

fraiseql-v-cache.label: FraiseQL · v+cache
fraiseql-v-cache.note: on-the-fly JSONB JOIN views + result cache

hasura.note: compiles GraphQL to a single SQL query

postgraphile.note: compiles GraphQL to a single SQL query

async-graphql.note: Rust per-level resolvers with DataLoader batching

mercurius.note: Fastify per-level resolvers with DataLoader batching

apollo-server.note: Node per-level resolvers with DataLoader batching

strawberry.note: Python per-level resolvers with DataLoader batching

F3.label: ORDER BY baseline (20 rows)
F3.note: duplicates Q1 until the orderBy variant lands; the cell keeps the grid complete

T1.label: Full blog page (multi-root)
T1.note: post + author + 10 comments-with-authors in one request; FraiseQL runs it multi-root

resolver-dataloader.label: Per-level batched resolvers
resolver-dataloader.summary: One HTTP hop, then the root SQL, then one BATCHED SQL per nesting level — each DataLoader coalesces a level's lookups into a single WHERE key = ANY($1) query, so there is no N+1. The residual cost is that those trips are serial (each level waits on the parent's ids) plus in-process resolver execution, so depth adds round-trips.

compile-to-sql.label: Compile the whole query to one SQL
compile-to-sql.summary: The engine compiles the entire GraphQL tree into ONE composed SQL statement (LATERAL joins / jsonb aggregation) and issues a single round-trip that returns the whole nested document — at any depth. Hasura, PostGraphile and FraiseQL's on-the-fly v views are all in this class; FraiseQL·v is one compiler among several, not a category of its own.

precompute.label: Read a pre-computed JSONB row
precompute.summary: The nested document is denormalised into a tv_* table at write time, so a read is a single SELECT of pre-built JSONB with no joins — one round-trip at any depth. On a result-cache hit (tv+cache) the database is not touched at all: the path stops at the server.

rest.label: Hand-written REST + SQL
rest.summary: No GraphQL document on the wire: each endpoint runs a hand-written SQL (a JOIN for the nested case) — one round-trip like a compiler, but bespoke per endpoint. Not one of the three animated GraphQL lanes; shown here for completeness.

anatomy.dataloader_credit: The classical GraphQL engines here are best-practice, not strawmen: every one batches its nested lookups with a DataLoader (WHERE key = ANY($1)), so there is no N+1 swarm. What the nesting cliff measures is the residual cost — the serial per-level round-trips plus in-process resolver execution — which is exactly what compile-to-SQL and precompute avoid.
anatomy.apq_note: APQ (automatic persisted queries) elides the document-upload work of the first hop: instead of sending the whole GraphQL query text, the client sends a 32-byte SHA-256 hash the server has already parsed. It shortens the request hop but changes no SQL round-trip; measured in the Q1_APQ / Q2b_APQ / M1_APQ cells.
anatomy.lens_note: These lanes are coloured by request mechanism, not by product family: FraiseQL·v is drawn in the compile-to-SQL lane because that is what it is, and only the pre-computed tv_* path stands apart.

variants.explain: Baseline: each read is compiled to on-the-fly JSONB JOIN views — no precompute, no result cache. The conservative starting point every other rung is measured against.
Adds a result cache in front of the JOIN-view path. On these varied list reads it earns almost nothing — the cache pays off on repeated hot-key lookups (see C3/HC3), not lists.
Switches reads to pre-computed tv_* rows built at write time: one SELECT of ready-made JSONB, no joins at read time. This is where the read speed comes from, and the gain widens as nesting deepens.
Adds the result cache on top of precompute — a small extra gain on an already-cheap read.

apq_rung.explain: Automatic persisted queries send a 32-byte hash instead of the query text. It shortens the request hop but changes no SQL — on these small documents it moves the needle little, and can cost a touch.
apq_rung.no_twin_note: no persisted-query twin was measured for this read in this run

mechanism_ladder.summary: Where the read speed comes from, one mechanism at a time. Each rung is the same read on the next FraiseQL variant; the bar is absolute throughput (from zero, so a flat rung looks flat) and the chip is its delta over the rung below. The result cache and APQ earn ~nothing on these list reads — the precompute step is the whole story, and it grows with depth.

apq.summary: APQ isolated: the same query sent as a pre-registered SHA-256 hash instead of full text. It changes no SQL round-trip, so it only helps when uploading and parsing the document is the bottleneck. In this run the read and write documents are small, so the measured APQ delta is near zero — sometimes slightly negative — and the chart shows that as-is. Frameworks with no first-party APQ handshake are greyed with their reason, never dropped.
apq.not_measured_note: APQ-capable, but its persisted-query twin was not measured in this run — distinct from excluded, and neither slow nor missing on purpose.

regimes.miss: C3 — 20 rotating UUIDs. Each request asks for a different row, so a result cache is cold on every request: the worst case a cache can face.
regimes.hit: HC3 — a 5-UUID hot pool. The same handful of rows repeat, so a result cache should serve almost every request from memory: the case caching is built for.

cache_under_fire.summary: Caching under fire: the same single-row lookup run two ways — against 20 rotating keys (C3, a cache can never hit) and against a 5-key hot pool (HC3, a cache should hit almost every time). The cache-off variants (v, tv) sit beside the cache-on ones (v+cache, tv+cache) on purpose: if the cache earned its keep, the cache-on rows would jump from C3 to HC3 while the cache-off rows stayed flat. In this run every row is flat — a single-row read is already so cheap (~4 ms) that caching the result saves almost nothing, hot pool or not, and tv+cache is a touch slower with the cache in the path. The chart shows that as-is.
cache_under_fire.not_measured_note: Wired in the benchmark but not run against the hot-key scenarios in this run — distinct from excluded, and neither slow nor missing on purpose.

cost.summary: The runs-on-a-toaster closer, priced honestly. This is the instance cost attributable to a million requests at the measured Q1 throughput, on the machine the sweep actually ran on (the CCX33 system-under-test). Because FraiseQL serves Q1 several times faster than the resolver engines on the same box, and in a fraction of their RAM, it costs a fraction per request — but these are derived figures (formula below), not a separate measurement.
cost.formula: € / 1M requests = price/month ÷ (measured Q1 RPS × 2,628,000 s) × 10⁶ — the instance cost attributable to a million requests at sustained throughput. Derived from the measured RPS and the dated price file, not itself measured; the same model as the report's cost composite. Meaningful because the sweep ran on this instance class (CCX33, the SUT); on other hardware it is a projection.
cost.price_note: Hetzner dedicated-vCPU pricing, EUR excl. VAT, from costs/instance-prices-2026-07.yaml (captured 2026-07-04). CCX33 = 8 dedicated vCPU / 32 GB.

rss.summary: Steady-state process memory, cold-start time and container-image size per framework. The FraiseQL variants sit around 11–13 MB; the Node and Python GraphQL servers run several times heavier, and hand-written Actix REST is lighter still. Shown as-is, no cherry-picking — Actix wins on RAM, but it serves a fifth of FraiseQL's Q1 throughput and speaks REST, not GraphQL.

footprint.db_summary: The trade the RAM-and-CPU win is paid with. FraiseQL's read speed comes from precomputed tv_* rows, and those rows cost disk: tv_comment is 4.4× the size of the tb_comment base table it derives from. The storage trade belongs to the same story as the footprint — cheaper memory and cores, more disk.

full.label: Full write
full.note: FraiseQL pays its full logged cascade (M1); classical engines a single vanilla UPDATE. The cascade fan-out count is not measured in this run, so the structural-count layer marks FraiseQL's write ‘fan-out not measured’ — the cost layer still uses its measured M1 service time.

delta.label: Delta / fast path
delta.note: Each engine's fast write path: FraiseQL's surgical jsonb-delta (M1d, one patch), classical's single vanilla UPDATE. M1d is measured only for fraiseql-tv in this run.

amortization.summary: The one system-level view — every story above is one request at a time, but a real service runs a mix of reads and writes. This models total sustainable load as that read:write ratio changes, and finds the break-even. FraiseQL moves read cost to write time (the cascade builds the precomputed rows), so it needs enough reads per write to amortize that write. A derived MODEL, not a measured cell — every input traces to a grid cell above.
amortization.cost_layer: Cost-weighted — the headline. Each engine's sustainable requests/second for a workload of 1 write + r reads, from measured throughput (1/read_rps per read, 1/write_rps per write, composed). At r→0 the curve is the measured write throughput; at r→∞ the measured read throughput. Higher is better; where FraiseQL's line crosses above a rival is the break-even for that pair.
amortization.count_layer: Structural query count — secondary, and counts are not cost. SQL round-trips per workload-unit from the S0 hop model: a per-level resolver does 2–3 trips for a nested read, a compiler or precompute does one. This is why depth hurts resolvers — but a round-trip is not a fixed price, so this layer never decides the winner, and it never leads.
amortization.caveat: A derived model on the median-of-three inputs, not a measured cell. Aggregation multiplies per-request numbers, so it compounds each cell's run-to-run spread (recorded in the run JSON); the read:write ratio is your assumption, shown across the whole range rather than one flattering point.

exclusion_reasons.1: M1d on v-variants — updateUserDelta patches the tvd_* delta tables of the tv pipeline; the v-variants serve on-the-fly JSONB views and have no delta pipeline to contrast (structural, see frameworks/fraiseql/database/extensions.sql).
exclusion_reasons.2: fraiseql-tv-audit — audit-overhead appendix row: measures M1 only, to isolate the cost of audit logging on the mutation path. Deliberately not a full-grid framework; do not expand.
exclusion_reasons.3: M1d on non-FraiseQL engines — the jsonb_delta/tvd_* surgical-patch mutation is FraiseQL infrastructure; no equivalent operation exists to benchmark elsewhere.
exclusion_reasons.4: APQ on Hasura — Hasura CE v2 has no automatic-persisted-query handshake (its allow-lists and query caching are different mechanisms / Enterprise features). Hand-rolling APQ would benchmark custom code.
exclusion_reasons.5: APQ on PostGraphile — v5 first-party persisted operations are a build-time allowlist, not the register-on-first-use sha256 handshake the APQ scenarios measure.
exclusion_reasons.6: APQ on actix-web-rest — APQ is a GraphQL wire-protocol optimization (persisting a query document by hash); REST requests carry no document, so the scenario is not applicable.
exclusion_reasons.7: APQ on Strawberry — Strawberry GraphQL ships no first-party APQ extension (verified against the installed strawberry/extensions inventory); third-party or hand-rolled implementations would not benchmark the framework.

read-heavy.label: Read-heavy
read-heavy.blurb: For read-heavy work the precomputed (tv) path wins: it tops the field at Q1, and its edge over FraiseQL's own JOIN-view (v) variants widens with nesting depth — level at Q1, decisive by Q3 — because precompute carries no N+1. Q1 is a strength here, not a soft spot; the cost of the precomputed document is paid on writes, not reads.

nested.label: Deeply nested
nested.blurb: The deeper the nesting, the wider FraiseQL's lead — no N+1 by construction. The cost of that read advantage is paid on writes, not reads (see the write trade).

write-heavy.label: Write-heavy
write-heavy.blurb: FraiseQL's delta path (M1d) competes with a classical single UPDATE; the full-cascade recompute (M1) is the price of always-consistent precomputed reads. MC1 needs one round-trip where classical needs two.

hot-key.label: Hot-key lookups
hot-key.blurb: A hot 5-key pool (HC3) is where a result cache should shine; the 20-UUID miss regime (C3) shows what a cache does when it cannot help. In this run both regimes land flat — the single-row read is already too cheap for the cache to matter.

notes.same_run: This page renders exactly one benchmark sweep. No cross-run or cross-hardware mixing — the generator refuses two JSON files. The numbers here are the per-cell median of three warm sweeps on one rented box; the first post-seed sweep is discarded as a warm-up, and each cell's run-to-run spread is in the run JSON.
notes.loadgen_headroom: The load generator (k6) runs on its own dedicated box and drives the system-under-test over a private network — never co-located, never sharing the SUT's cores. A pre-sweep headroom gate points k6 at a null target on the SUT and requires it to sustain far more than any framework serves (the enforced floor is 30,000 RPS, several times the fastest cell in this grid), so these numbers are server-bound, not load-generator-bound. The exact measured headroom and full topology are in the reproduction doc.
notes.logged_durability: The tv_* precomputed tables run LOGGED here — crash-durable, and the conservative choice for a published number. pg_tviews can run them UNLOGGED for more write throughput, but an unclean shutdown then truncates them; this run does not take that trade, so nothing here is inflated by dropping durability. The disk cost of precompute is shown honestly in S6.
notes.q1_toast: FraiseQL leads Q1 — its precomputed tv variants top the field here, not mid-pack. Each tv_user read still detoasts a full precomputed JSONB document, so the read-side cost is real; but in this run it is too small to surface — the tv variants sit level with their JOIN-view (v) siblings at Q1. The precompute trade is paid on writes (M1 → M1d), not on Q1 reads, and FraiseQL's read edge over its own v variants only widens as nesting deepens (Q2b → Q3).
notes.tview_scope: pg_tviews cascade triggers fire only while a FraiseQL framework is under test (tview_trigger_scope = fraiseql-only). Classical stacks run against a vanilla table with the triggers disabled, then tv_* rows are resynced before the next FraiseQL run.
notes.mc1_workflow: MC1 is a workflow benchmark, not raw server speed: it counts the client round-trips needed to reach a consistent state after a write. FraiseQL = 1 request/cycle (the mutation response carries the cascade); classical GraphQL and REST = 2 requests/cycle (mutation + serial re-fetch).
notes.m1_full_cascade: Under logged tviews, M1 triggers a full cascade recompute across the affected precomputed rows (61-row fan-out here) — the maintenance price of always-consistent precomputed reads.
notes.m1_delta: M1d measures the raw speed of FraiseQL's jsonb_delta patch step in isolation: the ecosystem's machinery patches only the changed fields of dedicated delta tables (tvd_*) in place, instead of recomputing — fast, and part of the tooling, not something you hand-write. Read it as the delta mechanism's speed, not a full integrated write: in this run M1d patches the tvd_* tables (the read that consumes them is postFullDelta), while the base row and the tv_* projection the main reads use are maintained on the M1 path — the full-cascade recompute. Bounds also: only this single-field update is exercised (inserts, deletes out of scope here), and at this throughput the write is server-bound, so M1d ties the quickest resolver engine rather than lapping it (the classical REST write measured also looks under-tuned, so that ceiling is soft).
notes.m1_vanilla: Classical M1 is a single UPDATE on a vanilla table with no derived state to maintain.
notes.tv_audit: fraiseql-tv-audit measures M1 only — an audit-overhead appendix row isolating the cost of audit logging on the mutation path. It is never a full-grid framework.
notes.not_measured: Cells marked “not measured in this run” are wired in the benchmark but were not executed in the run shown. They are distinct from “excluded by design” and are neither slow nor missing on purpose. This publishable run measured the full grid, so no cell carries this status.
